question: Tell me about a time you moved fast and took a scrappy shortcut in an R&D environment that you would never do on a flight system. Why was it the right call?
principle: Race on the racetrack, walk on ice

raiseTranscript.text: In our lab prototype for a sensor array, I skipped full regression testing and used a quick Python hack to bypass the safety interlock so we could iterate 3x faster on data collection. We logged it and reverted before any hardware handoff.
What made that the right call here?
The prototype was isolated, no flight software involved, and the risk was just our own time. We hit the milestone two weeks early and the team learned the failure modes faster.
Follow-up: How did you decide the boundary?
I checked with my lead first and we agreed it stayed in the lab only.

junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Race on the racetrack, walk on ice. Candidate described using a Python interlock bypass on an isolated lab prototype that they explicitly would never ship. They checked with their lead and logged the change, which kept the shortcut contained. This shows early understanding that R&D speed is acceptable only when risk is local and reversible. The story stayed at individual scope, which is appropriate for 0-2 years. Biggest strength is the clear boundary they drew between lab and flight without needing external prompting.

raiseTranscript.text: On a cross-team R&D demo for a new actuator controller, I green-lit a one-off wiring harness that bypassed two harness connectors to hit a customer showing. We documented it as non-flight and tore it down the next week.
How did you get the other teams aligned?
I ran a quick risk table in the shared doc and got the safety and firmware leads to sign off in one meeting. Everyone knew it stayed in the lab.

raiseTranscript.text: When our R&D group was six months behind on a new propulsion concept, I authorized a parallel bench test that used commercial off-the-shelf controllers instead of our flight-grade stack. We isolated it to one lab bay and required weekly reviews with the flight safety team.
We accepted a six-week slip on the main program to buy optionality on the new architecture. The bench data let us kill the concept early instead of carrying technical debt into flight development.

exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Race on the racetrack, walk on ice. The boundary was enforced at organizational scale. Biggest strength is the explicit linkage between the R&D shortcut and downstream flight risk reduction.
